concepts.title: Object Recognition Tasks and Definitions
concepts.one_liner: Object recognition involves various tasks like classification, localization, and segmentation, where the approach depends on how the question of identity is answered.
concepts.content:
There are many tasks that researchers use to address the problem of recognition. Although the ultimate goal is to tell what something it is by looking at it, the way that you will answer the question will change the approach that you will use. For instance, you could say, "That is a chair" and just point at it, or we could ask you to indicate all of the visible parts of the chair, which might be a lot harder if the chair is partially occluded by other chairs producing a sea of legs. It can be hard to precisely delineate the chair if we cannot tell which legs belong to it. In other cases, identifying what a chair is might be difficult, requiring understanding of its context and social conventions.

(see figure: What is a chair? The definition is based on affordances (i.e., something you can sit on) and on social conventions (i.e., some surfaces you can sit on are meant to be used to support other objects...)

In this chapter we will study three tasks related to the recognition of objects in images (classification, localization, and segmentation). We will introduce the problem definitions and the formulation that lays the foundations for most existing approaches.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognition is not a single problem but a suite of tasks. Understanding the nuances between simple identification and precise delineation is necessary to choose the right computational framework.
concepts.recap_md: - Recognition tasks include classification, localization, and segmentation.

concepts.title: Recognition-by-Components Theory

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Recognition-by-components theory suggests humans recognize objects by decomposing them into a small set of geometric parts called Geons.
concepts.content:
One important theory of how humans represent and recognize objects from images is the recognition-by-components theory proposed by Irving Biederman in 1987. He started motivating his theory with the experiment illustrated in (Figure 1.1.6). The first observation is that novel objects can be decomposed into parts, often at regions of sharp concavity. The second observation is that these parts resemble known geometric primitives.

(see figure: What is this? This drawing from Biederman @Biederman1987, shows a novel object. After looking at this drawing we can conclude the following: (1) we have never seen this object before, (2) it can be...)

Biederman postulated that objects are represented by decomposing the object into a small set of geometric components (e.g., blocks, cylinders, cones, and so on.) that he called **Geons**. He derived 36 different Geons that we can discriminate visually. Geons were defined by non-accidental attributes such as symmetry, colinearity, cotermination, parallelism, and curvature. An object is defined by a particular arrangement of a small set of Geons. Object recognition consists in a sequence of stages: (1) edge detection, (2) detection of non-accidental properties, (3) detection of Geons, and (4) matching the detected Geons to stored object representations.
concepts.motivation_md: This theory explains how humans can recognize an infinite variety of objects from a finite set of parts, even when seeing a novel object for the first time.
concepts.recap_md: - Objects are decomposed into 36 basic geometric primitives called Geons.

concepts.title: Compositionality in Vision

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Compositionality in vision refers to objects being formed by simpler, shared elements, though these components may vary in appearance across different classes.
concepts.content: One important aspect of his theory is that objects are formed by compositing simpler elements (Geons), which are shared across many different object classes. **Compositionality** in the visual world is not as strong as the one found in language, where a fix set of words are composed to form sentences with different meanings. In the visual world, components shared across different object classes will have different visual appearances (e.g., legs of tables and chairs share many properties but are not identical). Geons are great to represent artificial objects (e.g., tables, cabinets, and phones) but fail when applied to represent stuff (e.g., grass, clouds, and water) or highly textured objects such as trees or food.
concepts.motivation_md: Compositionality allows for efficient representation of the world; however, unlike language, visual components are often continuous and context-dependent, making a universal 'visual alphabet' difficult to define for natural textures.

concepts.title: Mental Rotation and Viewpoint Invariance

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Mental rotation is the hypothesized process where humans recognize objects in non-canonical poses by mentally rotating them to match a stored representation.
concepts.content:
One well studied property of the human visual system is its invariance to image and 3D rotations. Studies in human visual perception have shown that objects are recognized faster when they appear in canonical poses. In a landmark study, Roger N. Shepard and Jaqueline Metzler showed to participants pairs of drawings of three-dimensional objects. The result showed that participants had a reaction time proportional to the rotation angle between the two views. This supported the idea that participants were performing a **mental rotation** in order to compare both views.

(see figure: Two figures related by a 3D rotation. Modified from @Shepard1971aa)

Michael Tarr and Steven Pinker showed that similar results where obtained on a learning task. When observers learn to recognize a novel object from a single viewpoint they are able to generalize to new viewpoints but they do that at a cost: recognition time increases with the angle of rotation. When trained with multiple viewpoints, participants recognized equally quickly all the familiar orientations.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept explains why human recognition speed varies with viewpoint and suggests that our internal representations might be viewpoint-dependent rather than fully 3D-invariant.
concepts.recap_md: - Reaction time for recognition is proportional to the angle of rotation from a canonical or learned view.

slots.key_passage: - Reaction time for recognition is proportional to the angle of rotation from a canonical or learned view.

concepts.title: Levels of Categorization

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Categorization occurs at three levels of abstraction: superordinate, basic-level, and subordinate, allowing organisms to ignore irrelevant differences between stimuli.
concepts.content:
Categorization offers a number of advantages by allowing an organism not to differentiate one stimulus from others when that differentiation is irrelevant for the purposes at hand. Eleanor Rosch and her collaborators proposed that categorization occurs at three different levels of abstraction:

1. **Superordinate level**: Very general categories that provide a high degree of abstraction (e.g., Furniture, Tree).
2. **Basic level**: Corresponds to the most common level of abstraction (e.g., Chair, Oak).
3. **Subordinate level**: The most specific level of categorization (e.g., Kitchen chair, White oak).

Two objects belonging to the same superordinate category share fewer attributes than two objects belonging to the same subordinate category.
concepts.motivation_md: Categorization is essential for object recognition because it allows an organism to group equivalent objects together. By organizing information into levels of abstraction, we can efficiently process stimuli without being overwhelmed by irrelevant details.
concepts.recap_md: - Categorization happens at superordinate (general), basic (common), and subordinate (specific) levels.

concepts.title: Prototypes

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Prototypes are the clearest members of a category, used to define natural categories by their central examples rather than their fuzzy boundaries.
concepts.content: Natural categories tend to be fuzzy at their boundaries and inconsistent in the status of their constituent members. To address this, categories can be represented by prototypes, which are the clearest members of a category. Humans recognize categories by measuring the similarity of a stimulus to these prototypes. This approach makes it easier to work with continuous categories, as they are defined by "clear cases rather than its boundaries."
concepts.motivation_md: Natural categories often lack sharp boundaries. Prototypes provide a way to define and recognize categories based on central, ideal examples rather than rigid definitions.

concepts.title: Affordances and Contextual Meaning

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Object recognition is complicated by affordances, where an object's meaning or function changes based on the specific context in which it is used.
concepts.content:
Object recognition is not as straightforward as a simple categorization task because objects can have different affordances as a function of context. In linguistics, an expression has a standing meaning (its conventional definition) and an occasion meaning (its specific meaning in a particular context). The same principle applies to visual objects: an object's role can shift depending on its environment.

concepts.title: Image Classification Formulation
concepts.one_liner: Image classification is mathematically formulated as a function mapping an input image ${\bf x}$ to an output vector $\hat {\bf y}$ representing class presence.
concepts.content:
We can formulate image classification mathematically by building a function that maps the input image ${\bf x}$ into an output vector $\hat {\bf y}$: $$\hat {\bf y} = f({\bf x})$$ For a single object, the output $\hat {\bf y}$ is a binary response where $1$ indicates the object is present and $0$ indicates it is not.

(see figure: Image classification: Is there a car in this image?)

In general, we want to classify an image according to multiple classes. We can do this by having an output vector $\hat {\bf y}$ of length $K$, where $K$ is the number of classes. Component $c$ of the vector $\hat {\bf y}$ indicates whether class $c$ is present or absent in the image. A training set consists of images and their corresponding class indicator vectors.

(see figure: Image classification: Is there a car in this image?)
concepts.motivation_md: To perform automated object recognition, we need a formal mathematical framework that translates raw pixel data into structured labels identifying which objects are present.
concepts.recap_md: - Classification is modeled as a function $f({\bf x}) = \hat {\bf y}$.

concepts.title: Exclusive Classes in Image Classification
concepts.one_liner: Exclusive class classification assumes exactly one category is present in an image, constrained by the sum of output probabilities equaling one.
concepts.content: One common assumption in image classification is that only one class, among $K$ possible classes, is present in the image. This is typical in settings where most images contain a single large object. Multiclass classification with exclusive classes results in the following constraint: $$\sum_{c=1}^K \hat{y}_c=1$$
concepts.motivation_md: In many datasets, images are centered on a single primary subject. Enforcing an exclusivity constraint simplifies the model's decision-making process and reflects the structure of the data.

concepts.title: Simplex in Multiclass Classification
concepts.one_liner: In multiclass classification with exclusive classes, valid prediction vectors are constrained to lie within a simplex where components are positive and sum to one.
concepts.content:
In multiclass classification with $K$ exclusive classes, the valid solutions for the predicted vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=[\hat{y}_1, \hat{y}_2, \dots, \hat{y}_K]^\mathsf{T}$ are constrained to lie within a simplex, where $0 < \hat{y}_c < 1$.

Under this formulation, the classification function $f$ is a mapping $f:\mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 3} \rightarrow \vartriangle^{K-1}$ from the set of red-green-blue (RGB) images to the $(K-1)$-dimensional simplex, $\vartriangle^{K-1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: When classes are mutually exclusive, the model's output should represent a valid probability distribution. The simplex constraint ensures that individual class scores are bounded between 0 and 1 and collectively sum to 100%, preventing logically impossible predictions.

concepts.title: Softmax Regression Model
concepts.one_liner: The softmax regression model interprets the output of a function as a probability mass function over $K$ classes.
concepts.content:
The softmax regression model produces an output $f_{\theta}$ that can be interpreted as a probability mass function over $K$ classes:

$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(Y \bigm | \mathbf{x}) &= \hat{\mathbf{y}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \end{aligned}$$

where $Y$ is the random variable indicating the single class per image. This relates to the classification probability model as:

$$\begin{aligned} p(Y_c=1 \bigm | \mathbf{x}) &= p_{\theta}(Y=c \bigm | \mathbf{x}) \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Softmax regression allows a neural network to output a categorical probability distribution, making it suitable for multi-class decision making where we need to know the model's confidence in each mutually exclusive category.
concepts.recap_md: - Interprets the output vector as a probability mass function over $K$ classes.

concepts.title: Multilabel Classification
concepts.one_liner: Multilabel classification treats the problem as $K$ independent binary classification tasks where an image can belong to multiple classes simultaneously.
concepts.content:
When an image can have multiple labels simultaneously, the classification problem can be formulated as $K$ binary classification problems, where $K$ is the number of classes. 

In such a case, the function $f_\theta$ can be a neural network shared across all classes, and the output vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ of length $K$ is computed using a sigmoid nonlinearity for each output class. The output can still be interpreted as the probability $\hat{y}_c = p_\theta(Y_c=1 \bigm | \mathbf{x})$, but without the constraint that the sum across classes is 1.

(see figure: Multilabel image classification system.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard multiclass classification assumes only one label is correct. Multilabel classification is necessary for complex scenes where multiple objects (e.g., a car, a person, and a tree) are present and all need to be identified.

concepts.title: Misclassification Error
concepts.one_liner: Misclassification error is a measure of classification performance defined as the total number of incorrect class predictions across a dataset.
concepts.content:
In order to learn the model parameters, we define a loss function to capture the task. One natural measure of classification error is the misclassification error. The errors that the function $f$ makes are the number of misplaced ones over the dataset, which can be written as:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{c=1}^{K} \mathbb{1}(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \neq y^{(t)}_c ). \end{aligned}$$

where $T$ is the number of images in the dataset.
concepts.motivation_md: Misclassification error provides a direct, intuitive count of how many times the model was wrong. While useful for evaluation, its discrete nature makes it difficult to use directly for gradient-based optimization.
concepts.recap_md: - Measures the total count of incorrect predictions across all classes and samples.

concepts.title: Cross-Entropy Loss for Exclusive Classes
concepts.one_liner: Cross-entropy loss for exclusive classes is the negative log-likelihood of the ground truth labels, commonly used for differentiable optimization in image classification.
concepts.content:
If we interpret the function $f$ as estimating the probability $p(Y_c=1 \bigm | {\bf x}) = \hat{y}_c$, with $\sum_c \hat{y}_c =1$, the likelihood of the ground truth data is:

$$\prod_{t=1}^T \prod_{c=1}^K \left( \hat{y}^{(t)}_c \right) ^{y^{(t)}_c}$$

where $y^{(t)}_c$ is the ground truth value of $Y_c$ for image $t$. Maximizing this likelihood corresponds to minimizing the cross-entropy loss, obtained by taking the negative log of the likelihood, resulting in a total classification loss:

$$\mathcal{L}_{cls}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} y^{(t)}_c \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c)$$

The cross-entropy loss is differentiable and is commonly used in image classification tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Unlike raw misclassification error, cross-entropy is a smooth, differentiable function. This allows for the use of gradient descent to optimize model parameters by penalizing the model based on the confidence of its predictions.
concepts.recap_md: - Derived from maximizing the likelihood of the ground truth data.

concepts.title: Multiclass Binary Cross-Entropy Loss
concepts.one_liner: Multiclass binary cross-entropy loss is used for non-exclusive labels by applying a sigmoid layer and summing individual binary cross-entropy losses for each class.
concepts.content:
If classes are not exclusive, the likelihood of the ground truth data is:

$$\prod_{t=1}^T \prod_{c=1}^K \left( \hat{y}^{(t)}_c \right) ^{y^{(t)}_c} \left( 1-\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \right) ^{1-y^{(t)}_c}$$

where the outputs $\hat{y}_c$ are computed using a sigmoid layer. Taking the negative log of the likelihood gives the multiclass binary cross-entropy loss:

$$\mathcal{L}_{cls}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} y^{(t)}_c \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c) + (1-y^{(t)}_c) \log(1-\hat{y}^{(t)}_c)$$

concepts.title: Top-1 Performance
concepts.one_liner: Top-1 performance measures the percentage of times the true class label matches the highest-scored prediction.
concepts.content:
Classification performance uses the output of the classifier, $f$, as a continuous value (the score $\hat{y}_c$) for each class. We can rank the predicted classes according to that value. The top-1 performance measures the percentage of times that the true class-label matches the highest scored prediction, $\hat{y} = \underset{c}{\mathrm{argmax}} ( \hat{y}_c )$, in the test set:

$$\text{TOP-1} = \frac{100}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{1}( \hat{y}^{(t)} = y^{(t)})$$

where $y^{(t)}$ is the ground truth class of image $t$. This evaluation metric only works for the exclusive class case since it assumes a single ground truth class per image. For the multilabel case, we may instead check if each label is predicted correctly.
concepts.motivation_md: Top-1 accuracy is the most standard and rigorous metric for classification, requiring the model to identify the single correct category as its most confident prediction.
concepts.recap_md: - Measures how often the highest-probability prediction is correct.

concepts.title: Top-5 Performance
concepts.one_liner: Top-5 performance measures the percentage of times the true label is among the five highest-scoring predictions.
concepts.content: In some benchmarks (such as ImageNet), researchers measure the top-5 performance, which is the percentage of times that the true label is within the set of five highest scoring predictions. Top-5 is useful in settings where the labels might be ambiguous, or where multiple labels for one image might be possible. The top-5 measure is less precise and it is used when the test set only contains one label despite that multiple labels might be correct. In the case of multiple labels, ideally, the test set should specify which labels are possible and evaluate only using those.
concepts.motivation_md: In large-scale datasets with hundreds of categories, some labels are very similar (e.g., different breeds of dogs). Top-5 performance provides a more lenient evaluation that accounts for such ambiguity or the presence of multiple valid objects in a single-label dataset.

concepts.title: Confusion Matrix
concepts.one_liner: The confusion matrix summarizes the overall performance of a classifier and the percentage of times that classes are confused with one another.
concepts.content:
For multiclass prediction problems, it is often useful to look at the structure of mistakes made by the model. The confusion matrix summarizes both the overall performance of the classifier and the percentage of times that two classes are confused. The diagonal elements represent the top-1 performance for each individual class, while the off-diagonal elements show the specific confusions. For instance, a classifier might confuse cats as dogs more frequently than other categories.

(see figure: Confusion matrix for a three-way classification task. The numbers are percentages.)

The elements of the confusion matrix are defined as:

$$C_{i,j} = 100 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}( \hat{y}^{(t)} = j)  \mathbb{1} (y^{(t)} = i)}{\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}(y^{(t)} = i)}$$

where $C_{i,j}$ measures the percentage of times that true class $i$ is classified as class $j$. In a typical example, 80 percent of cat images might be correctly classified, while 5 percent are classified as cars and 15 percent are classified as dogs.
concepts.motivation_md: In multiclass classification, simple accuracy doesn't reveal which specific classes the model struggles to distinguish. The confusion matrix provides a granular view of error patterns, helping developers identify if the model is systematically misidentifying one class as another.

concepts.title: Object Localization
concepts.one_liner: Object localization consists of localizing where an object is in an image, typically by finding a tight bounding box around it.
concepts.content: For many applications, saying that an object is present in the image is not enough. For example, in a visual system for an autonomous vehicle, simply knowing a person is in the image is insufficient for deciding how to navigate. Object localization consists of localizing where the object is in the image. There are many ways to specify where the object is. The most traditional way of representing the object location is using a bounding box, which involves finding the image-coordinates of a tight box around each instance of class $c$ in the image $\bf x$.
concepts.motivation_md: Classification only identifies *what* is in an image; localization is necessary to determine *where* those objects are, which is critical for tasks like robotics, autonomous driving, and image editing.
concepts.recap_md: - Localization identifies the specific spatial coordinates of objects within an image.

concepts.title: Bounding Box
concepts.one_liner: A bounding box is a set of image coordinates defining a tight box around an object instance.
concepts.content: The most traditional way of representing an object's location is using a bounding box. This involves finding the image-coordinates of a tight box around each of the instances of class $c$ in the image $\bf x$.

concepts.title: Object Localization Formulation
concepts.one_liner: Object localization is formulated as a function mapping an image to a list of bounding boxes and their associated class vectors.
concepts.content:
Object detection is formulated as a function that maps the input image ${\bf x}$ into a list of bounding boxes $\hat {\bf b}_i$ and the associated classes to each bounding box encoded by a vector $\hat {\bf y}_i$.

(see figure: Car localization using bounding boxes. Each instance is shown with a different color.)

The class vector, $\hat {\bf y}_i$, has the same structure as in the image classification task but is applied to describe each bounding box. Bounding boxes are usually represented as a vector of length 4 using either the coordinates of the two corners, ${\bf b} = [x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2]$, or the center coordinates, width, and height, ${\bf b} = [x_c, y_c, w, h]$. The goal is to find a function $f$ such that: $${ \hat {\bf y}_i, \hat {\bf b}_i } = f({\bf x})$$

concepts.title: Three Steps of Object Detection
concepts.one_liner: Most object detection approaches involve proposing candidate boxes, classifying the patches within them, and postprocessing to remove redundancies.
concepts.content: Most approaches for object detection have three main steps. In the first step, a set of candidate bounding boxes are proposed. In the second step, we loop over all proposed bounding boxes, and for each one, we apply a classifier to the image patch inside the bounding box. In the third and final step, the selected bounding boxes are postprocessed to remove any redundant detections.
concepts.motivation_md: Processing every possible rectangular area in an image is computationally impossible; this three-step pipeline breaks the problem into manageable stages of proposal, verification, and refinement.

concepts.title: Window Scanning Approach
concepts.one_liner: The window scanning approach turns classification into detection by sliding a classifier across the image at multiple scales.
concepts.content:
In its simplest form, the problem of object localization is posed as a binary classification task, namely distinguishing between a single object class and the background class. Such a classification task can be turned into a detector by sliding it across the image (or image pyramid) and classifying each local window.

concepts.title: Selective Search
concepts.one_liner: Selective search efficiently proposes candidate bounding boxes using a fast selection mechanism before applying a more expensive classifier.
concepts.content:
The window scanning approach can be slow as the same classifier needs to be applied to tens of thousands of image patches. Selective search makes the process more efficient by proposing an initial set of bounding boxes that are good candidates to contain an object. This proposal mechanism is performed by a selection mechanism simpler than the object classifier.

(see figure: Selective search pipeline.)

This approach was motivated by the strategy used by the visual system in which attention is first directed toward image regions likely to contain the target. This first attentional mechanism is very fast but might be wrong; therefore, a second, more accurate but also more expensive, processing stage is required to take a reliable decision. The advantage of this cascade of decisions is that the most expensive classifier is only applied to a sparse set of locations, dramatically reducing the overall computational cost.

The algorithm for selective search only differs from the window scanning approach in how the list of candidate bounding boxes is generated. Some approaches also add a bounding box refinement step.

concepts.title: Selective Search Pipeline
concepts.one_liner: The selective search pipeline uses a four-step process of candidate generation, classification, refinement, and nonmaximum suppression to detect objects in images.
concepts.content:
This algorithm consists of four main steps. First, it uses an efficient window scanning approach to produce a set of candidate bounding boxes. Second, the algorithm loops over these candidate boxes, crops and resizes them to a canonical size, and applies an object classifier to determine if the crop contains the target object. Third, the bounding boxes for crops classified as containing the object are refined. Finally, low-scoring boxes are removed and nonmaximum suppression (NMS) is used to discard overlapping detections likely to correspond to the same object, ensuring only one bounding box is output for each instance.

(see figure: A first classifier selects candidate bounding boxes. A second, stronger, classifier makes the final detections (e.g., cars). Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) removes overlapping detections.)

The classification and bounding box refinement, $f_1$, are implemented by a classifier and a regression function.

concepts.title: Nonmaximum Suppression (NMS)
concepts.one_liner: Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) is an iterative algorithm used to discard overlapping bounding boxes and output a single detection for each object instance.
concepts.content:
Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) is used to discard overlapping detections likely to correspond to the same object, so as to output only one bounding box for each instance present in the image. The algorithm takes as input a set of object bounding boxes and confidences, $S=\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}_{i=1}^B$, and outputs a smaller set by removing overlapping boxes. 

It is an iterative algorithm as follows: 
(1) Take the highest confidence bounding box from the set $S$ and add it to the final set $S^*$.
(2) Remove from $S$ the selected bounding box and all the bounding boxes with an IoU larger than a threshold.
(3) Go to step 1 until $S$ is empty.
concepts.motivation_md: Detectors often produce multiple overlapping bounding boxes for the same object. NMS provides a systematic way to select the most confident box and suppress redundant detections based on spatial overlap.

concepts.title: Cascade of Classifiers
concepts.one_liner: A cascade of classifiers divides object search into a sequence of functions with increasing computational complexity and accuracy.
concepts.content:
Trying to localize an object in an image is difficult because the object is usually small and surrounded by a complex background. Selective search reduces this complexity by dividing the search into two steps: a fast, cheap classification function to detect candidate locations, and a slow, expensive function to accurately classify the object in those subsets. A cascade of classifiers pushes this idea to the limit by dividing the search into a sequence of classifiers of increasing computational complexity and accuracy.

(see figure: Cascade of classifiers algorithm.)
concepts.motivation_md: Localizing objects is like finding a needle in a haystack. Cascades allow systems to quickly reject obvious background regions using simple tests, saving expensive computations for the most promising and difficult areas of the image.

concepts.title: Viola-Jones Face Detector
concepts.one_liner: The Viola-Jones detector is a ground-breaking real-time face detector based on a cascade of boosted classifiers introduced in 2001.
concepts.content: Cascades of classifiers became popular in computer vision when Paul Viola and Michael Jones introduced them in 2001 with a ground-breaking real-time face detector based on a cascade of boosted classifiers. In parallel, Fleuret and Geman also proposed a system that performs a sequence of binary tests at each location, where each test checks for the presence of a particular image feature. Early versions of this strategy were inspired by the game "Twenty Questions."
concepts.motivation_md: Before this approach, real-time face detection was computationally prohibitive. The Viola-Jones detector proved that a cascade of simple features could achieve high accuracy with enough speed for live video applications.

concepts.title: Computational Allocation in Cascades
concepts.one_liner: In a cascade, computational power is concentrated on image regions likely to contain the target object while flat regions are rejected quickly.
concepts.content:
In a cascade, computational power is allocated into the image regions that are more likely to contain the target object, while regions that are flat or contain few features are rejected quickly with almost no computations. This results in a heat map of computational cost where the intensity is proportional to the number of levels in the cascade applied to each location.

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)
concepts.motivation_md: Uniformly processing every pixel in an image is wasteful. This approach ensures that the 'computational budget' is spent where it matters most—on complex regions that resemble the target object.

concepts.title: YOLO (You Only Look Once)
concepts.one_liner: YOLO (You Only Look Once) is an object detection approach that makes predictions by looking at the image globally for higher computational efficiency.

concepts.title: Object Localization Loss
concepts.one_liner: Object localization loss combines classification loss and localization loss to evaluate how well a detector identifies and places bounding boxes.
concepts.content:
The object localization loss accounts for two complementary tasks: classification and localization. 

- Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$): Measures if the predicted label matches the ground truth for a detected bounding box.
- Localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$): Measures how close the detected location is to the ground truth object location.

To evaluate an image, the detector's output set of bounding boxes $\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}_{i=1}^B$ is associated with ground truth labels $\{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}_{i=1}^B$. Predicted boxes overlapping with ground truth are optimized to improve locations and labels. Boxes that do not overlap are assigned to the background class ($\mathbf{y}_i=0$), and the model is optimized to reduce their predicted class scores $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$. Multiple detections can be assigned to the same ground truth box.

(see figure: (left) Detector output (using a low threshold to generate many detections). (middle) Ground truth bounding boxes (one color per instance). (right) Detector outputs that overlap with ground truth...)
concepts.motivation_md: Object detection requires knowing both 'what' an object is and 'where' it is. A specialized loss function is needed to simultaneously penalize incorrect labels and imprecise spatial coordinates.

concepts.title: Classification Loss
concepts.one_liner: Classification loss measures whether the predicted label for a detected bounding box matches the ground truth using cross-entropy.
concepts.content:
Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$) evaluates whether the predicted label matches the ground truth at a specific location for each detected bounding box. Since each bounding box can only belong to one class, cross-entropy loss is used:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) = - \sum_{c=1}^{K} y_{c,i} \log(\hat{y}_{c,i})$$

where $K$ is the number of classes.
concepts.motivation_md: In object detection, once a region is proposed, the model must decide which category it belongs to. Cross-entropy loss provides a differentiable way to maximize the probability assigned to the correct class.

concepts.title: Precision
concepts.one_liner: Precision is the percentage of correct detections among all positive predictions for a given threshold.
concepts.content:
From the quantities of detections and ground truth, we compute the precision as the percentage of correct detections:

$$
Precision(\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)}
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Precision measures the accuracy of a model's positive predictions, helping to quantify how often a detection is actually correct rather than a false alarm.
concepts.recap_md:
- Precision calculates the ratio of true positives to the total number of predicted positives.
- It is computed for a specific decision threshold $\beta$.

concepts.title: Recall
concepts.one_liner: Recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances that are correctly detected for a given decision threshold.
concepts.content:
Recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances that are detected for a given decision threshold $\beta$:

$$Recall (\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i \mathbf{y}_i}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Recall is used to determine how well a model finds all relevant instances in a dataset, highlighting the impact of misdetections or false negatives.
concepts.recap_md:
- Recall is the ratio of correctly detected instances to the total number of actual ground truth instances.
- It quantifies the model's ability to avoid missing detections.

concepts.title: Average Precision (AP)
concepts.one_liner: Average precision (AP) summarizes the entire non-monotonic precision-recall curve as the area under the curve.

concepts.motivation_md: Since precision and recall change with different thresholds, AP provides a single, comprehensive metric to evaluate a model's performance across all possible thresholds.

concepts.title: Stuff vs. Objects
concepts.one_liner: The distinction between 'stuff' (unbounded regions like sky) and 'objects' (discrete instances) helps determine appropriate image representations.
concepts.content:
It is useful to differentiate between stuff and objects. Stuff refers to things that do not have well-defined boundaries such as grass, water, and sky. However, the distinction between stuff and objects is not very sharp. In some images, object instances might be easy to separate, like the two trees in the left image below, or become a texture where instances cannot be detected individually (as shown in the right image). In cases with lots of instances, bounding boxes might not be appropriate and it is better to represent the region as "trees" than to try to detect each instance.

(see figure: Bounding boxes are not an appropriate representation of the location of trees. This is true for many object classes with extended shapes that are hard to approximate with a box.)
concepts.motivation_md: Differentiating between stuff and objects helps researchers choose between semantic segmentation (for stuff) and instance detection (for objects), especially when bounding boxes fail to capture amorphous shapes.

- 'Stuff' refers to entities without well-defined boundaries like grass or sky.
- 'Objects' are discrete instances, though the boundary between stuff and objects can be blurry depending on the image context.

concepts.title: Multiclass Semantic Segmentation Loss
concepts.one_liner: The multiclass semantic segmentation loss is the cross-entropy loss applied to every pixel across all classes and training examples.
concepts.content:
Training this function requires access to a dataset of segmented images. Each image in the training set will be associated with a ground truth segmentation, $y^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right]$ for each class $c$. The multiclass semantic segmentation loss is the cross-entropy loss applied to each pixel:

$$\mathcal{L}_{seg}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} \sum_{n,m}  y^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right] \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right])$$

where the sum is over all the training examples, all classes, and all pixel locations. This loss might focus too much on the large objects and ignore small objects. Therefore, it is useful to add a weight to each class that normalizes each class according to its average area in the training set.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard cross-entropy allows for pixel-wise classification, but class weighting is often necessary to prevent the model from being biased toward large, frequent background classes like 'sky' or 'road'.
concepts.recap_md:
- The loss is calculated as a pixel-wise cross-entropy sum across all classes and images.
- Class weighting is recommended to ensure small objects are not ignored in favor of large ones.

concepts.title: Mean IoU for Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Mean IoU provides a scale-invariant measure of segmentation quality by averaging the Intersection over Union across all classes.
concepts.content: In order to evaluate the quality of the segmentation, we can measure the percentage of correctly labeled pixels. However, this measure will be dominated by the large objects (sky, road, etc.). A more informative measure is the average IoU across classes. The IoU is a measure that is invariant to scale and will provide a better characterization of the overall segmentation quality across all classes.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple pixel accuracy is misleading because a model can achieve high scores by only predicting large background classes; Mean IoU forces the model to perform well on all classes regardless of their size.
concepts.recap_md:
- Mean IoU averages the Intersection over Union metric across all object classes.
- It is preferred over pixel accuracy because it is invariant to the scale of objects in the image.

concepts.title: Instance Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Instance segmentation combines object detection and semantic segmentation to output localized objects as pixel-level masks.
concepts.content:
We can combine the ideas of object detection and semantic segmentation into the problem of instance segmentation. Here the idea is to output a set of localized objects, but rather than representing them as bounding boxes we represent them as pixel-level masks as shown in @fig-instance_segmentation.

concepts.motivation_md: Instance segmentation is needed when we need to distinguish between individual occurrences of the same class (e.g., separate cars) while also knowing their precise shapes.
concepts.recap_md:
- It identifies individual object instances and provides a unique mask for each.
- It differs from semantic segmentation by distinguishing between different instances of the same class.

concepts.title: Instance Segmentation Pipeline
concepts.one_liner: Instance segmentation can be achieved by applying a binary semantic segmentation function to the cropped image within each proposed and labeled bounding box.
concepts.content:
One approach to instance segmentation is to follow the object localization pipeline but, after the bounding boxes have been proposed and labeled, feed the cropped image within each bounding box to a binary semantic segmentation function. This function predicts, for each pixel in box $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$, whether it belongs to the object or not, resulting in an instance mask for each box. Such an approach was introduced in @he2017. The architecture is illustrated in @fig-instance_segmentation_architecture.

concepts.title: Instance Segmentation Loss
concepts.one_liner: The instance segmentation loss combines classification, localization, and segmentation losses into a single weighted objective function.
concepts.content:
The loss can be written as a combination of the classification, localization, and segmentation losses:
$$
\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\})
     =  \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) +
     \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)
     \left( 
     \lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)
     +
     \lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}} (\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i, \mathbf{s}_i)
     \right)
$$

The first classification loss corresponds to the classification of the crop as containing the object or not. If the object is present, the second term measures the accuracy of the bounding box, and the third term measures whether the segmentation, $\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i$, inside each bounding box matches the ground truth instance segmentation, $\mathbf{s}_i$. The parameters $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ control how much weight each loss has on the final loss.

concepts.title: Limitations of Language-Based Object Recognition
concepts.one_liner: Language-based object representations are often insufficient for robotics and autonomous systems that require 3D modeling, physical properties, and dynamic understanding.
concepts.content:
The representations described in this chapter feel incomplete for applications like robotics or autonomous vehicles, where object representations are hard to act on. A robot planning to grasp an object needs accurate 3D modeling and an understanding of physical properties to plan grasping points. Similarly, autonomous vehicles require 3D descriptions of object locations and their dynamics. Therefore, object segmentation and classification provide only part of the necessary information.

Techniques relying on language to define objects (e.g., tagging, captioning) leave many questions unanswered, such as:
- Is this piece of matter an object or a random arrangement?
- What is its 3D shape and how is it supported?
- What are its mechanical properties (soft, rigid, deformable)?
- How will it react to external actions or grasping?
- What is its utility or physical origin?
- Is it stable or alive?

A computer vision system should behave as a scientist, formulating hypotheses and performing experiments to answer these questions. While language can answer some, it does not need to be the only internal representation used.

concepts.title: Localization Loss
concepts.one_liner: Localization loss measures how close a detected location is to the ground truth object location.
concepts.content: Localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$) measures how close the detected location is to the ground truth object location. It is used to quantify the error in the predicted bounding box coordinates $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$ relative to the actual coordinates $\mathbf{b}_i$.
concepts.motivation_md: In object detection, identifying that an object exists is not enough; we must also accurately determine its spatial position. Localization loss provides a differentiable metric to optimize the precision of predicted bounding box coordinates during training.
concepts.recap_md: - Localization loss measures the spatial discrepancy between predicted and ground truth bounding boxes.

concepts.title: Intersection over Union (IoU)
concepts.one_liner: Intersection over Union (IoU) is a typical measure of similarity between two bounding boxes.
concepts.content: A typical measure of similarity between two bounding boxes is the Intersection over Union (IoU). [FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.] The IoU is a quantity between 0 and 1, where 0 indicates no overlap and 1 indicates that both bounding boxes are identical.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard distance metrics like L2 distance don't account for the area of overlap relative to the total area covered. IoU provides a normalized metric that intuitively represents how well two boxes align regardless of their absolute size.
concepts.recap_md: - IoU measures the overlap between two bounding boxes as a value between 0 and 1.

concepts.title: IoU Loss
concepts.one_liner: IoU loss is defined as one minus the Intersection over Union between predicted and ground truth bounding boxes.
concepts.content: Since IoU is a similarity measure, the localization loss can be defined as: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1-IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}).$$ The IoU is translation and scale invariant, and it is frequently used to evaluate object detectors. However, the IoU loss becomes 1 when the two bounding boxes do not overlap, which means that there will be no gradient information when running backpropagation.
concepts.motivation_md: While IoU is a good evaluation metric, it needs to be converted into a loss function for training. By using $1 - IoU$, we create a minimization objective that is scale-invariant, though it suffers from vanishing gradients when boxes don't overlap.
concepts.recap_md: - IoU loss is calculated as $\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} = 1 - IoU$.

concepts.title: L2 Regression Loss
concepts.one_liner: L2 regression loss is a simple optimization objective that sums the squared differences of bounding box coordinates.
concepts.content: A simpler loss to optimize than IoU is the L2 regression loss: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$ The L2 regression loss is translation invariant, but it is not scale invariant; the loss is larger for big bounding boxes. concepts.title: Overall Localization Loss
concepts.one_liner: The overall loss combines classification and localization losses, weighted by a parameter and an indicator function.
concepts.content: The overall loss is computed by combining the classification and the localization loss: $$ \mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) + \lambda \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0) \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i) $$ where the indicator function $\mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)$ sets to zero the location loss for the bounding boxes that do not overlap with any of the ground truth bounding boxes. The parameter $\lambda$ can be used to balance the relative strength of both losses. This loss makes it possible to train the whole detection algorithm end-to-end, although it is also possible to train the localization and classification stages independently.
concepts.motivation_md: Object detection requires solving two tasks simultaneously: identifying what an object is and where it is. A multi-task loss function allows the model to optimize both objectives in a single training pass.
concepts.recap_md: - The total loss is the sum of classification loss and a weighted localization loss.

concepts.title: Precision-Recall Evaluation
concepts.one_liner: The most common approach for evaluating object localization is measuring the average precision-recall.
concepts.content: There are several ways of evaluating object localization approaches. The most common approach is measuring the average precision-recall. Just as when defining the localization loss, we need to assign detection outputs to ground truth labels. This assignment can be done in several ways, and they can result in different measures of performance. The methodology introduced in the PASCAL challenge used a specific procedure for this assignment.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple accuracy is insufficient for object detection because it doesn't account for the trade-off between finding all objects (recall) and ensuring detections are correct (precision).
concepts.recap_md: - Average precision-recall is the standard metric for evaluating object localization.

concepts.title: Assigning Detections to Ground Truth Labels
concepts.one_liner: Detections are assigned to ground truth labels by matching high-confidence boxes to the highest IoU ground truth.
concepts.content: To assign detections to ground truth labels, first sort all detections by their score, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$. Then, loop over the sorted list in decreasing order. For each bounding box, compute the IoU with all ground truth bounding boxes and select the one with the highest IoU. If the IoU is larger than a predefined threshold (typically 0.5), mark the detection as correct and remove that ground truth bounding box from the list to avoid double counting. If the IoU is below the threshold, mark the detection as incorrect and do not remove the ground truth label. Repeat until all detections are evaluated, and mark any remaining ground-truth bounding boxes as missed detections.
concepts.motivation_md: In evaluation, we need to know which predicted box corresponds to which real object. This greedy matching process ensures that each object is only counted once and that high-confidence predictions are prioritized.
concepts.recap_md: - Detections are matched to ground truth boxes based on the highest IoU above a threshold.

concepts.title: Precision-Recall Curve
concepts.one_liner: The precision-recall curve measures the performance of the detection as a function of the decision threshold.
concepts.content: The precision-recall curve measures the performance of the detection as a function of the decision threshold $\beta$. As each bounding box comes with a confidence score $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$, the threshold $\beta$ is used to decide if an object is present at the bounding box location $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$. Given a threshold $\beta$, the number of detections is $\sum_i \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)$ and the number of correct detections is $\sum_i \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i$. Both precision and recall are quantities between 0 and 1, where high values correspond to high performance. (see figure: Example of a precision-recall curve. This is a standard plot to evaluate detection algorithms. It is usually summarized by the area under the curve. In this example, note that recall stops around...)
concepts.motivation_md: A single precision or recall value only describes performance at one specific threshold. The curve shows the full trade-off, allowing researchers to see how the model behaves across all possible confidence levels.
concepts.recap_md: - The curve plots precision against recall as the confidence threshold $\beta$ varies.
